units.title: Unit 17 — Business
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 17. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Business: starting companies, customer relationships and market performance
learningObjectives: Describe starting, launching, expanding and supplying a business, including business plans and custom-built products.
Explain market research, potential customers, customer care, order books, competition and profits.
Use business collocations such as put forward a plan, make a profit, build contacts and face stiff competition.
Recognise intransitive business uses of sell, launch and roll out and distinguish countable business from uncountable business, feedback and competition.

sectionsChecked: A: Starting a business; word definitions and Language help
B: Common business English phrases and collocations; Common mistakes

items.example: She started a small business that designs software for schools.
items.note: Countable when referring to one enterprise; compare uncountable business as commercial activity.

items.example: The founder put forward a plan to improve the online shop.
items.note: Put forward a plan or proposal means present it so others can consider it.

items.example: The investors asked to see a business plan before offering any money.
items.note: A document describing how a proposed business will operate and earn money.

items.pt: feito sob medida; fabricado conforme especificações
items.example: They ordered a custom-built workstation for video editing.
items.note: Designed or built for a particular customer's requirements; the book uses this adjective with computers.

items.example: She bought a custom-made desk for her home office.
items.note: A close alternative to custom-built; listed as an acceptable answer in Exercise 17.1.

items.example: The team plans to launch a business next spring.
items.note: Launch means begin operations, often with a public announcement; contrast expand an existing business.

items.example: The company will launch a lighter laptop later this year.
items.note: A company launches a product, but a product can also launch without an expressed object in business English.

items.pt: lançar; disponibilizar gradualmente ou em larga escala
items.example: The company will roll out the new service across the country next month.
items.note: A new product or service can also roll out without an explicit object in business English.

items.example: The manufacturer introduced an expanded range of small devices.
items.note: Range means a selection of products; expanded means made larger.

items.pt: expandir uma empresa; ampliar os negócios
items.example: They intend to expand the business into several neighbouring countries.
items.note: Expand is the verb; an expanded range uses its past-participle adjective.

items.example: The expansion will create more jobs in the region.
items.note: Noun from expand; expansion does not itself mean the launch of an entirely new company.

items.example: The firm specialises in equipment for research laboratories.
items.note: A business or company, often used in formal and professional contexts.

items.example: The factory manufactures specialist electronic components.
items.note: Manufacture usually refers to producing goods in significant quantities, often in a factory.

items.example: The manufacturer checks every unit before shipping it.
items.note: A person or company that makes goods; related to the verb manufacture.

items.example: The supplier delivers orders to customers throughout Europe.
items.note: In this context, deliver goods means transport them to the buyer.

items.pt: atendimento ao cliente; cuidado com o cliente
items.example: Excellent customer care helped the small company retain loyal buyers.
items.note: Typically uncountable; concerns the way a company responds to and helps its customers.

items.example: The workshop offers personal service rather than automatic replies.
items.note: Attention tailored to an individual's needs, not merely a personal favour.

items.example: Keeping customer information safe is our highest priority.
items.note: Something considered more important or urgent than competing concerns.

items.example: They carried out market research before developing the new product.
items.note: Research is uncountable here; do market research, not a market research.

items.example: Before entering a new market, the company carried out market research.
items.note: Natural verb phrase with uncountable research; do market research is also possible.

items.example: Many firms reduced spending during the recession.
items.note: A period of weak economic activity, often accompanied by difficult trading conditions.

items.example: The team interviewed potential clients before investing.
items.note: An adjective for something possible in the future; not the same as an existing customer.

items.example: The advertisement reached thousands of potential customers.
items.note: Someone who might purchase something if circumstances are right.

items.example: Starting without enough savings can be a serious risk.
items.note: The possibility of an undesirable result; take a risk and worth the risk are common phrases.

items.pt: que vale o risco; que compensa arriscar
items.example: She believed the investment was worth the risk.
items.note: Worth + noun describes something whose expected benefit justifies the danger or uncertainty.

items.pt: carteira de pedidos; registro de encomendas
items.example: After the trade fair, the company's order books were full.
items.note: Plural expression for orders received but not yet completed; not literally only printed books.

items.example: Going forward, we will provide updates every two weeks.
items.note: Common business discourse marker for future action, not an expression of physical movement.

items.pt: um produto vende; tem saída no mercado
items.example: The new headphones sell well because they are affordable.
items.note: Sell can be used without a direct object when saying how readily a product finds buyers.

items.pt: um produto é lançado; chega ao mercado
items.example: The updated model launches in September.
items.note: Business usage can make the product itself the subject of launch, without itself or a passive construction.

items.pt: um serviço é lançado; passa a ser disponibilizado
items.example: The upgraded payment service rolls out next week.
items.note: The product or service may be the subject; avoid a reflexive pronoun such as rolls itself out.

items.example: We hope to do more business overseas next year.
items.note: Uncountable when referring to commercial activity: more business, not more businesses in this sense.

items.example: We do business with several suppliers in South America.
items.note: Refers to commercial dealings; business is uncountable in this expression.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: The CEO presented the company's priorities at the meeting.
items.note: CEO stands for Chief Executive Officer, usually the most senior executive.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: The corporation operates in more than twenty countries.
items.note: Often a large company or related group of companies managed as one organisation.

items.pt: entrar em novos mercados; alcançar novos mercados
items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: Reliable local distributors helped the company access new markets.
items.note: Here access is a verb followed directly by the market; it does not require access to.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: The firm intends to enter the market with a low-cost product.
items.note: Enter is a transitive verb: enter a market, not enter to a market.

items.pt: criar contatos profissionais; desenvolver uma rede de contatos
items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: She built contacts at international engineering conferences.
items.note: Build contacts means establish useful professional relationships, not construct physical objects.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: The company made a profit after its second year of trading.
items.note: Use make a profit, not make money as a one-to-one equivalent in every context.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: The firm's profit increased even though sales stayed stable.
items.note: Money gained after costs; distinguish profit from revenue or sales.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: Small businesses face stiff competition from online retailers.
items.note: Stiff means strong or intense here, not physically rigid.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: Competition from larger manufacturers has increased.
items.note: Uncountable when referring generally to commercial rivalry: face competition, not competitions.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: The development team used customer feedback to fix the design.
items.note: Uncountable in this sense: some feedback or a piece of feedback, not a feedback.

items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: We get feedback from users after each product release.
items.note: Common collocation for collecting opinions from customers or colleagues.

items.pt: opiniões dos clientes; retorno dos clientes
items.section: B · Common business phrases and collocations
items.example: Customer feedback revealed that the instructions were unclear.
items.note: Feedback often concerns the experience of using a product or service.

items.example: The design agency asked its client to approve the final proposal.
items.note: Exercise 17.2 uses clients; compare customer, especially a buyer of goods or services.

units.title: Unit 18 — Sport
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 18. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Sport: disciplines, equipment, athletics, competitions and participants
learningObjectives: Identify sports illustrated in the unit and choose correct names for sporting equipment.
Discuss athletics events, sprinters, long-distance runners and marathons.
Use set a record, hold a record, qualify for, get knocked out and reach a semi-final accurately.
Differentiate sportsperson names such as canoeist, mountaineer, archer and gymnast and use British sports equipment.

sectionsChecked: B: Equipment; C: Athletics, figures and text
D: Competition in sport; E: People who do particular sports; Common mistakes

items.example: She tried hang-gliding during a holiday on the coast.
items.note: Air sport using a lightweight wing; different from paragliding.

items.example: They went ten-pin bowling after work.
items.note: The ball is rolled towards ten pins; ten-pin distinguishes it from other bowling forms.

items.example: My sister joined a fencing club at university.
items.note: Sport involving sword-like weapons; a participant is a fencer.

items.example: The rider competed in showjumping for the first time.
items.note: Horses and riders complete a course of obstacles.

items.example: He enjoys windsurfing when there is a steady breeze.
items.note: Combines a board with a sail; distinct from surfing without a sail.

items.example: We watched a snooker match on television.
items.note: Cue sport using coloured balls; rules differ from pool and billiards.

items.example: They played a game of pool after dinner.
items.note: Cue sport played with balls on a table; not identical to snooker.

items.example: My grandfather taught me how to play billiards.
items.note: Umbrella term or a specific cue-sport variant depending on context; plural in form.

items.example: He follows motor racing but rarely watches other sports.
items.note: Competitive racing in vehicles powered by motors; may include several categories.

items.pt: snowboard; prática de descer na neve com prancha
items.example: Snowboarding requires excellent balance on steep slopes.
items.note: Sport performed on a single board on snow, rather than two skis.

items.pt: mergulho com equipamento autônomo de respiração
items.example: They went scuba diving near a coral reef.
items.note: Uses underwater breathing equipment, unlike simple snorkelling.

items.example: Archery demands a steady hand and careful aim.
items.note: Sport of shooting arrows with a bow; participant: archer.

items.example: He selected a golf club for the long shot.
items.note: Club is the equipment, not a sports association in this context.

items.example: My tennis racket broke during the match.
items.note: Equipment used to hit a ball or shuttlecock in tennis, badminton or squash.

items.example: One dart landed just outside the centre of the board.
items.note: Small pointed object thrown at a dartboard; plural darts names the sport.

items.example: The archer checked her bow before the competition.
items.note: Used in archery; paired with an arrow.

items.example: The batter raised the bat before the first pitch.
items.note: Used in baseball, cricket and table tennis; distinguish from golf club and hockey stick.

items.example: Each player needs a hockey stick and protective equipment.
items.note: Used in ice or field hockey to control and strike the puck or ball.

items.example: He used a cue to strike the white ball.
items.note: The stick used in cue sports such as pool and snooker.

items.example: She held the paddle firmly while guiding the canoe.
items.note: A paddle is not fixed to the boat, unlike an oar in many rowing boats.

items.example: The rower pulled the oar through the water.
items.note: An oar is usually supported by the boat as it is used; contrast paddle.

items.example: He bought a fishing rod for his weekend trip.
items.note: Rod is the long flexible pole; line is the thin material attached to it.

items.example: The fishing line snapped when the fish pulled hard.
items.note: Fishing uses a rod and line; they name different parts of the equipment.

items.example: She has trained in athletics since secondary school.
items.note: In British English, athletics includes track-and-field events; US athletics can refer more broadly to sports.

items.example: He practised the discus throw with a coach.
items.note: Field event in which an athlete throws a heavy disc as far as possible.

items.example: The athlete picked up the discus before the throw.
items.note: Discus is the implement; discus throw names the event.

items.pt: lançamento de dardo (modalidade); dardo de atletismo
items.example: She won the javelin with a throw of over fifty metres.
items.note: Can refer to the throwing event or the long pointed implement.

items.example: She improved her personal best in the high jump.
items.note: Athletes jump over a horizontal bar; not the same as long jump.

items.example: He trains for the long jump twice a week.
items.note: Athletes try to jump as far as possible from a take-off point.

items.example: Gymnastics requires flexibility and strength.
items.note: A sport involving controlled physical movements; gymnastics is not the word for a person.

items.example: The pole vault event was delayed by heavy rain.
items.note: Athletes use a long flexible pole to clear a high bar.

items.example: The young sprinter hopes to compete at a national level.
items.note: Someone who runs short distances at high speed; related verb: sprint.

items.example: The long-distance runner trains on hilly roads every morning.
items.note: Races over greater distances; contrast sprinter.

items.example: She completed her first marathon in just over four hours.
items.note: A race of 42.195 kilometres; do or run a marathon are natural.

items.example: The swimmer set a record at the regional championships.
items.note: Set a record = achieve a new best performance, often in a measured event.

items.example: She still holds the record for the fastest junior race.
items.note: Hold a record describes being its current recognised owner; set describes establishing one.

items.example: He broke an Olympic record during the final.
items.note: A record achieved in the Olympic Games; distinct from a world record.

items.example: The new world record attracted international attention.
items.note: Best officially recognised performance worldwide in a particular event.

items.example: Her favourite swimming event is the 100-metre breaststroke.
items.note: A swimming stroke with characteristic arm and leg movements.

items.example: Their national team managed to qualify for the tournament.
items.note: Qualify for a competition means meet the conditions to take part.

items.example: Our team got knocked out in the quarter-finals.
items.note: Often followed by in + round or of + competition; not the same as physical unconsciousness.

items.example: The team lost in the second round.
items.note: A stage of a competition; do not confuse with the shape adjective round.

items.pt: conseguir chegar até; alcançar uma etapa
items.example: The team made it to the final despite several injuries.
items.note: Informal expression meaning succeed in reaching a stage or destination.

items.example: Their club reached the semi-final for the first time.
items.note: Reach takes a direct object; do not use reach to the semi-final.

items.example: The semi-final takes place on Thursday.
items.note: Round immediately before the final in a knockout tournament.

items.example: They lost the final on penalties.
items.note: The deciding stage of a competition; not the same as semi-final.

items.example: The defending champions were beaten in the first round.
items.note: Be beaten means lose to an opponent; beat someone is the active form.

items.example: The regional league has become increasingly competitive.
items.note: May describe a contest with strong rivalry or a person eager to win.

items.example: The captain lifted the trophy after the match.
items.note: A prize awarded to winners, often a cup or decorative object.

items.example: The referee stopped the match after a dangerous tackle.
items.note: Official responsible for enforcing the rules; not always called an umpire.

items.example: Several thousand spectators attended the athletics event.
items.note: A spectator physically watches an event; contrast TV viewer or a fan following a team.

items.example: The fans celebrated the team's unexpected victory.
items.note: A fan supports a team or athlete; does not have to be present at an event.

items.example: The footballer joined the club last summer.
items.note: A sportsperson formed with -er from football.

items.example: The swimmer practises every morning before work.
items.note: A person who swims; for competition contexts, swimmer is a normal label.

items.example: The tennis player won in straight sets.
items.note: Use tennis player, not tenniser; player also works for badminton and squash.

items.example: The squash player recovered quickly after a difficult match.
items.note: With squash, use player rather than a made-up suffix.

items.example: The canoeist navigated the narrow river carefully.
items.note: Standard spelling includes -e-: canoeist, not canoist.

items.example: The mountaineer reached the summit before noon.
items.note: A person who climbs mountains; not mountainer.

items.example: The jockey wore bright colours during the horse race.
items.note: A professional horse rider in racing, not necessarily an equestrian showjumper.

items.pt: arqueiro; praticante de tiro com arco
items.example: The archer practised aiming at distant targets.
items.note: Practises archery; the word is archer, not archerer.

items.example: The gymnast performed an impressive routine.
items.note: Person doing gymnastics; gymnast, not gymnastic.

items.example: The golfer practised putting before the match.
items.note: Golfer is the correct person noun, not golfist.

items.example: All sports equipment must be checked before training.
items.note: British English normally uses plural sports before equipment, club or facilities.

items.section: Exercises · Sporting equipment and match vocabulary
items.example: The archer placed an arrow against the bowstring.
items.note: Exercise 18.2 names the arrow as equipment associated with archery.

items.section: Exercises · Sporting equipment and match vocabulary
items.example: She hung a dartboard on the wall of the games room.
items.note: Exercise 18.2 identifies a dartboard as the target used in darts.

items.section: Exercises · Sporting equipment and match vocabulary
items.example: The runner received a silver medal at the championships.
items.note: Exercise 18.3 mentions medals as individual awards, distinct from trophies.

items.section: Exercises · Sporting equipment and match vocabulary
items.example: The referee showed a red card after the foul.
items.note: Exercise 18.3 uses the disciplinary card shown by a referee in football.
